title: How does a calorimeter work? - heat from a reaction, a temperature change, and what a calorimeter measures
summary: A guided virtual experiment for beginners: the student pours the water, places the reaction, inserts the thermometer, closes the calorimeter and runs the reaction, while a lab guide explains each result - leading to ΔT, q = mcΔT, heat loss, the bomb calorimeter (q_V = ΔU), constant pressure (q_p = ΔH) and ΔH − ΔU = Δn_g RT.
subject: Chemistry
subtopics: Heat from a reaction warms the surrounding water
A thermometer measures the temperature change, not heat
Heat taken in by water: q = mcΔT
Bomb calorimeter: constant volume, q_V = ΔU
Constant pressure: q_p = ΔH; ΔH − ΔU = Δn_g RT
concepts: A calorimeter finds heat indirectly, from the temperature change of a known amount of material
Insulation keeps the heat in so the measurement is fair
q = mcΔT: the same heat warms more water by less
A sealed bomb cannot expand, so q_V = ΔU; at constant pressure q_p = ΔH
learningObjectives: Explain how heat capacity links the heat supplied to a system to its rise in temperature.
Calculate the heat needed to change the temperature of a sample from its mass or amount and its specific or molar heat capacity.
Explain why a bomb calorimeter measures the change in internal energy of a reaction.
Compare measurements at constant volume and at constant pressure, and the quantity each one gives.
Calculate the energy change of a reaction from the temperature change and heat capacity of a calorimeter.

verification.note: Concept exploration for beginners; simple illustrative numbers (2100 J, c = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ as in NCERT; 30 % loss in the uninsulated run is illustrative). Awaiting owner review.

interactivity: 13 scenes, each opened by the student's own action
pour the water, place the reaction tube, insert the thermometer, close the lid
inspect the lid, insulation, water, thermometer and tube
start the reaction and read ΔT
build q = mcΔT from m, c and ΔT; change m and ΔT
inspect the bomb, push its wall, ignite the sample
push a piston, run a gas-forming reaction
lab guide: what you did, what happened, why, next
